opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, partly because I give a lot of advice. I write these long posts on getting into mechanistic interpretability, I mentor a bunch of people, and I've had loads of one-on-one calls. The honest answer is that I try to hold it all pretty loosely.

The core limitation is that advice is lossy compression of one person's experience and the people they've happened to observe. When I say "here's how to get into research," I'm drawing on my path, my MATS scholars, and people I've worked with at DeepMind and elsewhere. That's a real data set, but it's skewed. The people who reach me are already selected for being keen, often technical, often in a particular part of the world, and the people I hear back from are disproportionately the ones it worked out for. So there's survivorship bias baked in.

The other big thing is that the right advice often depends on which direction someone is already erring in. A classic example: I'll tell people "just start doing research, stop reading papers forever, get your hands dirty." That's exactly right for a perfectionist who's spent six months preparing and never feels ready. But a small fraction of people are already reckless. They dive in, don't learn the basics, and produce sloppy work. If they hear "just go do stuff," it pushes them further the wrong way. Broadcast advice can't see who's listening, so I try to frame things as "if you're the kind of person who does X, consider Y," and to point out the opposite failure mode too.

On usefulness, I think the bar is lower than people assume. It doesn't need to be perfectly calibrated. It needs to make people aware of options and considerations they hadn't thought of, and then let them apply their own judgment. A lot of my value is saying out loud the tacit knowledge experienced researchers have: that it's normal for most ideas not to work, that you should spend a day or two on a quick and dirty experiment before committing for months, that it's fine to email people you admire. That stuff is surprisingly hard to get unless you're in the right lab or the right group chat, and writing it down levels the playing field a bit.

The field also moves fast, especially in AI safety and interpretability. Something I said two years ago about which research directions are promising may simply be wrong now. I've changed my mind on things fairly publicly, for example becoming more skeptical of some of the more ambitious "fully reverse-engineer the model" framings and more pragmatic about what interpretability can deliver. So I'd tell anyone to check the date on my advice and treat older takes as historical context rather than gospel.

My general meta-advice is: collect advice from several people who disagree, figure out why they disagree, and treat it as hypotheses to test cheaply on yourself. You're the one with the most information about your situation. I'm happy to be one input, just not the only one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, honestly, because I've written a bunch of career advice posts and I'm aware that a lot of people read them, and I have this nagging worry that some fraction of readers are going to take something I said way too literally and make a worse decision because of it.

The core problem is that any advice I give is a generalisation. It's drawn from my experience, which is the experience of one person who happened to get into mechanistic interpretability at a particular moment, had a particular set of skills and circumstances, and got pretty lucky along the way. And then I'm talking to an audience that's incredibly varied: people with PhDs, people who are undergrads, people who've been software engineers for a decade, people who are complete beginners. There's no single piece of advice that's correct for all of those people. So when I say something like "just go do a research project and write it up," that's great advice for a lot of people and terrible advice for someone who doesn't yet have the basic coding skills to do that, or who's actually in a position where they should just apply for a specific role rather than spending six months on self-directed work.

The way I try to handle this is a few things. One is I try to be explicit about who I think the advice is for and what assumptions I'm making. Two, I try to give the reasoning behind the advice rather than just the conclusion, because if people understand why I'm recommending something, they can check whether that reasoning actually applies to their situation. Someone who knows "Neel thinks writing up your work matters because it's a legible signal to hiring managers who are time-constrained" can evaluate that themselves far better than someone who just heard "write stuff up."

And three, I try to flag my own biases. I think I'm more bullish on mechanistic interpretability than the field average, I have survivorship bias, I came up in a period where the field was tiny and it was much easier to get noticed than it is now. I think a lot of advice from people who are successful is implicitly "do the thing I did," and the thing they did might have worked specifically because of the time and place.

The limitation I'm most worried about is that advice tends to be received as more confident than it's intended. I'll say "I think probably X," and people hear "Neel says X." Which is partly just an inevitable property of putting things in writing to a large audience, and I think the right response is to keep saying out loud: this is one data point, you should talk to other people, you should weigh it against your own knowledge of yourself. If someone reads something I wrote and it makes them think more clearly about their own situation, great. If it replaces their own thinking, that's a failure, even if the advice was good.

r004.rationale: It describes the audience as varied, but does not identify selection toward certain kinds of people in Neel’s research experience as a limit on generalizing his advice.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing is to treat my advice as one data point, rather than as a verdict. I have a particular set of experiences, and those give me useful intuitions about some things, but they also create blind spots. And when I’m giving advice to a broad audience, I don’t know your circumstances, your strengths, or what you’ve already tried.

Research advice is often easier to assess by trying it on a small scale. If I suggest a way to choose projects or get feedback, you can ask: does this actually help me make progress? Career advice is harder, because the decisions are bigger and the feedback is slower. There, I’d want you to compare several perspectives and look for cheap ways to test the assumptions behind the advice.

And I think it’s useful to distinguish between me explaining why I believe something and me sounding confident about it. Ideally, the explanation lets you work out whether it applies to you. You shouldn’t have to take my confidence on trust.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is that advice is a pretty lossy compression of someone’s experience. I can tell you what I’ve seen work, particularly in mechanistic interpretability, but that’s a fairly narrow slice of the world. And the people who come to me are a selected sample, so even within that slice, I don’t necessarily see what happens to everyone who follows the advice.

I’d want people to treat it as a source of hypotheses rather than as a verdict. If I say that doing a small research project is a good way to test your fit, you can try that and learn something. If I say that you probably need some particular trait to be a good researcher, I’d be much more cautious about using that to rule yourself out. My ability to predict who will do good research is limited, and you can often get much better evidence by actually trying.

The difficulty with giving advice to a broad audience is that different people need opposite advice. Some people need to be more ambitious and stop waiting for permission; others need to narrow their project and finish something. So I try to explain why I believe something and who I think it applies to. Ideally, you come away better able to make the decision yourself, rather than just thinking, ‘Neel said I should do this.’
